statement: In laboratory studies in which adults first sampled a benzodiazepine and a dummy pill (placebo) and then chose which to take, a history of problem drug use (the papers' 'drug abuse') is associated with choosing the benzodiazepine: volunteers without such a history mostly chose the placebo, and diazepam calmed and sedated them without raising euphoria scores, while people with such a history almost always chose the benzodiazepine, though they were tested in separate studies by another laboratory, mostly at much higher doses, so their history and the dose cannot be told apart. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team (each kind of person was studied mainly by one laboratory, and no study read compared people with and without such a history at the same doses). In the one primary study read (de Wit et al., 1986, University of Chicago), 36 paid volunteers aged 21 to 35, recruited through advertisements and posters on a university campus and by word of mouth, told that the study offered money and not treatment, and excluded if they had a history of problem drug use, major depression, bipolar disorder or schizophrenia (12 without anxiety, 11 with anxious mood and 13 with generalized anxiety disorder; 6 others did not finish, one of them because of diazepam's sedative effects), each took part in three experiments in counterbalanced order: diazepam (Valium) 5 mg, diazepam 10 mg and d,l-amphetamine 5 mg, each against a placebo capsule of another colour (study conditions). They swallowed one capsule between 9 and 10 in the morning and then went about their day; after four sampling sessions they chose which colour to take on five more occasions. Most chose the placebo: at 5 mg, 21 of the 36 chose diazepam at most once and 8 chose it four or five times; at 10 mg, 27 chose it at most once and 5 four or five times (the numbers fell across the choice categories: z = −2.2, P < .03, and z = −3.0, P < .004), whereas 20 of the 36 chose amphetamine four or five times (z = 2.3, P < .02). The anxious groups chose no differently from the others, but with 11 to 13 people a group only large differences could have been seen (editors' note). Among people who liked one capsule better during the sampling sessions, more liked the placebo: 17 against 8 at 5 mg and 21 against 9 at 10 mg (editors' sums from Table 5). Diazepam lowered ratings of anxiety, vigour and arousal and raised ratings of confusion and sedation, 10 mg also raised fatigue, and on 10 mg days depression and dysphoria scores were higher and friendliness, elation and positive mood scores lower than on placebo days; the euphoria scale did not change significantly at either dose, while amphetamine raised it. Most people recognised 10 mg diazepam as a tranquilizer (30 of 36). The volunteers were not new to drugs (29 of the 36 had used marijuana, 19 stimulants and 6 tranquilizers outside medical care, and 9 drank more than 7 drinks a week; editors' sums from Table 2), but choice was not analysed by drinking or drug history. The authors' conclusion that highly anxious people are not at greater risk of dependence goes beyond what was tested, single morning doses on separate days; they add that people in acute distress, people less bothered by sedation, people expecting a particular effect and people with much earlier sedative or alcohol use might respond differently. A narrative review of laboratory studies published up to 1997, by two authors at Johns Hopkins University (Griffiths & Weerts, 1997; no stated search; its figures are second-hand here, as the primary papers were not read), calls a person's history the most important single factor in whether a benzodiazepine is chosen. In 13 studies of people with 'histories of drug abuse' (2 to 16 people each, men in all but one, 11 of the 13 co-authored by the review's first author; editors' counts from Table 2 and the reference list), the benzodiazepine was almost always chosen, or taken more than its comparison: for example, 16 men chose diazepam over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% of occasions; but four of the 13 studies had no placebo comparison (editors' count), triazolam was taken more than placebo by 4 of 6 men in one study, and in another all 8 men chose triazolam before a relaxation task and none before a vigilance task. In 17 studies of people without such histories (12 with de Wit or Johanson of the Chicago group among the authors; editors' count), healthy volunteers who were light drinkers without anxiety or insomnia consistently did not choose a benzodiazepine over placebo (for example diazepam on 25% to 38% of choice sessions in four studies, lorazepam on 16% and flurazepam on 20%), in several studies choosing it significantly less often than placebo, while amphetamine was chosen under similar conditions. Most of the studies in people with histories of problem drug use gave much higher doses (for example diazepam 40 to 400 mg in three of them, against diazepam in single doses of 2 to 20 mg or in 4 mg capsules taken one at a time in the studies of other volunteers; study conditions), and the review itself reports that choice depended on dose, yet it does not discuss dose as an explanation of the difference between the two kinds of people (editors' reading). What the review counts as a drug being chosen for its effects (reinforcement) covers any reason, whether to feel good, to ease anxiety or to avoid withdrawal, so choosing a benzodiazepine does not by itself show that people felt high. Moderate social drinkers (about 12 drinks a week) chose diazepam over placebo in three studies, on 100%, 73% and 64% of choices, while light drinkers (about 4 a week), tested under the same procedure in two of them, did not significantly prefer it (66%, a non-significant tendency, and 40%; the difference from moderate drinkers significant in the second); the moderate drinkers more often used marijuana weekly, and the review says that people with a history of moderate drinking or of alcoholism showed greater positive mood effects from benzodiazepines (no figures given), while calling what the drinkers' preference means for real-life risk unclear. In anxious people the results were mixed and lined up with how the drug was offered: two studies with a single morning dose found no preference (de Wit et al., 1986, and 14 people seeking treatment, who chose diazepam on 37% of sessions), while three that let people decide when and how many capsules to take found one (65% of evening sessions in 22 anxious volunteers against 45% in 23 volunteers without anxiety, P = 0.06; 3 of 4 women with generalized anxiety disorder, and 11 of 14 people with generalized anxiety or panic disorder, taking capsules as needed over 4 weeks, mostly at low, stable rates). People with insomnia chose triazolam on 86% of nights when they had to pick it or a placebo at bedtime, but took placebo capsules as often as triazolam when either was simply on offer. The review flags its comparisons across studies as not tested prospectively. As cited by the review, about half of US high-school students who reported non-medical use of tranquilizers (mostly benzodiazepines) said they usually got high from them (a survey report covering 1975 to 1992, with no single year given). In a US national survey of 2015 and 2016, getting high was the main reason given by 11.6% of adults who reported misusing benzodiazepines, behind relaxing and sleep (see the answer on why people misuse benzodiazepines). The laboratory studies date from 1976 to 1997, are small, used capsules prepared by the researchers, and none that the review describes followed whether choosing a benzodiazepine in the laboratory predicts later use outside it.
plain: Do benzos get you high, and who likes them? In lab studies, it depended on who people were. In one study, 36 young volunteers with no history of drug problems, though most had tried cannabis, took diazepam (Valium) or a dummy pill on different mornings and then chose which one to take, five more times. Most chose the dummy pill: at the higher of two doses, 27 of the 36 picked diazepam once at most. It calmed them and made them sleepy and a bit muddled, and it did not raise their euphoria scores; at the higher dose they also felt more tired and less cheerful and friendly than after the dummy pill. Volunteers with anxiety chose it no more often than the others, though it eased their anxiety. A review of older lab studies, whose figures are second-hand here, found that people with a history of drug problems almost always chose benzos over a dummy pill, but they were tested in other labs' studies, mostly at much bigger doses, so it can't be told whether their history made the difference. Moderate drinkers chose diazepam more often than light drinkers, and anxious people chose benzos when they could take capsules as they felt they needed them. Outside labs, some people report getting high: the review cites a US school survey in which about half of students who used tranquilizers without a prescription said they usually got high, and in a 2015–16 US survey 12 in 100 adults who misused benzos named getting high as their main reason.
population: Adults in laboratory choice studies: in the primary study read, 36 paid volunteers aged 21 to 35 at the University of Chicago without a history of problem drug use (12 without anxiety, 11 with anxious mood and 13 with DSM-III generalized anxiety disorder; 22 women); as summarized second-hand by a narrative review of studies published up to 1997, people with histories of problem drug use (13 studies of 2 to 16 people, men in all but one) and people without (17 studies: healthy volunteers, light and moderate social drinkers, people with or without an alcoholic first-degree relative, anxious people, people with insomnia); for context, US adults reporting benzodiazepine misuse in a 2015–2016 national survey
exposure: A benzodiazepine given by the researchers by mouth, mostly double-blind, in capsules of a colour that people learned during sampling sessions (study conditions: in the primary study single morning doses of 5 or 10 mg diazepam on separate days; in the review's studies diazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam, oxazepam, triazolam or flurazepam, mostly at much higher doses in people with histories of problem drug use, for example diazepam 40 to 400 mg in three studies, and diazepam in single doses of 2 to 20 mg or in 4 mg capsules taken one at a time in others)
comparator: Placebo capsules in the same people (a choice between the two colours, or self-administration of each); kinds of people compared across separate studies (problem drug use or not) and within some studies (anxious or not; moderate or light drinkers); d,l-amphetamine 5 mg as a comparison drug in the primary study
outcome: How often the benzodiazepine was chosen or taken rather than placebo; liking ratings; identification of the capsule; mood questionnaires (Profile of Mood States; the ARCI questionnaire with euphoria, sedation and dysphoria scales); for context, the main reason for misuse people gave in a national survey
magnitude: de Wit et al. (1986), 36 people (controls 12, anxious mood 11, generalized anxiety disorder 13), numbers choosing the drug on 0–1, 2–3 and 4–5 of 5 choice sessions: diazepam 5 mg 21, 7, 8 (trend z = −2.2, P < .03); diazepam 10 mg 27, 4, 5 (controls 9, 1, 2; anxious mood 10, 1, 0; generalized anxiety 8, 2, 3; z = −3.0, P < .004); d,l-amphetamine 5 mg 6, 10, 20 (z = 2.3, P < .02); no group differences. Editors' shares: diazepam at most once 58 in 100 (5 mg) and 75 in 100 (10 mg), four or five times 22 and 14 in 100; amphetamine four or five times 56 in 100. Mean amphetamine choices 4.0, 3.1 and 2.9 of 5 (controls, anxious mood, generalized anxiety), about 67% overall (editors' calculation from the printed means; the review's Table 3 estimates 73%). Liking over the sampling sessions (Table 5; equal ratings left out): placebo liked more by 17 and diazepam by 8 at 5 mg (11 equal); by 21 and 9 at 10 mg (5 equal; 35 of the 36 accounted for); choice by liking z = 2.51 (P < .02) at 5 mg; at 10 mg placebo chosen more whichever capsule was liked more, z = 2.63 (P < .01). Identification: 10 mg diazepam called a tranquilizer by 30 of 36, 5 mg by 18 of 32. Mood (Table 6): both doses lowered Anxiety, Vigor, Arousal and the stimulant-like BG scale and raised Confusion and the sedation (PCAG) scale (drug by hour, P = .001 to .04); 10 mg raised Fatigue (P = .001), Depression (P = .03) and the dysphoria (LSD) scale (P = .01) and lowered Friendliness (P = .004), Elation (P = .003) and Positive Mood (P = .003); no significant diazepam effect on the euphoria (MBG) scale; amphetamine on MBG drug by hour P = .001. Background (Table 2; editors' sums): marijuana ever 29, stimulants ever 19, tranquilizers outside medical care ever 6, more than 7 drinks a week 9, of 36. Griffiths & Weerts (1997), as tabulated (second-hand): people with histories of problem drug use, 13 studies, 2 to 16 people each; diazepam chosen over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% (16 men); lorazepam chosen over buspirone by 7 of 8; triazolam a reinforcer in 4 of 6, and chosen before relaxation by 8 of 8 and before a vigilance task by 0 of 8; 4 of 13 studies without a placebo comparison (editors' count). People without such histories, 17 studies: diazepam 28% and 27% of choice sessions (5 and 10 mg; 10 people), 25%, 32% and 38% (three groups), 28% (estimated, de Wit et al., 1986), 33% (43 people); lorazepam 2 mg 16% and flurazepam 30 mg 20% (12 people each); 5 mg d-amphetamine 76%. Moderate against light social drinkers (about 12 against 4 drinks a week): 100% against 66% (12 and 18 people), 73% against 40% (14 and 13; difference significant); moderate drinkers 64% diazepam (30 people) against 27% buspirone (25 others). Anxious people: 37% (14 seeking treatment, single morning dose); 65% against 45% (22 and 23 people; P = 0.06); 3 of 4; 11 of 14. Insomnia: triazolam on 86% of nights under forced choice (three groups of 8); capsules on 77% (triazolam) and 80% (placebo) of nights when only one was available. As cited: about half of US high-school students reporting non-medical tranquilizer use usually got high. Maust et al. (2019): main reason for benzodiazepine misuse to get high 11.6% (13.9% at ages 18–49, 3.0% at 50 or older), against relaxing 47.1% and sleep 26.6%.

evidence.locator: Subjects and Methods › Subjects, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Instructions and Consent; Procedure, 1st–3rd paragraphs (p. 534); Results › Subject Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (p. 535)
evidence.extracted: 42 paid volunteers aged 21–35 recruited through the student newspaper, campus posters and word of mouth (advertisements for the anxious groups asked whether the reader felt anxious, tense or nervous), told the study offered money, not treatment; excluded: serious medical problems, a history of problem drug use ('drug abuse' in the paper), or a history of major depression, bipolar disorder or schizophrenia (DSM-III). 36 completed: 12 controls, 11 with anxious mood and 13 with DSM-III generalized anxiety disorder (mean ages 26, 27 and 27; men 6, 4 and 4); 6 did not complete (three controls, three anxious mood), five for personal reasons and one control because of diazepam's sedative effects. Three experiments in counterbalanced order: d,l-amphetamine 5 mg, diazepam 5 mg and diazepam 10 mg (Valium and Benzedrine tablets in opaque capsules filled with dextrose), each against a dextrose placebo capsule; three sessions a week for three weeks, the capsule taken between 9 and 10 am, after which people were free to leave; four sampling sessions (drug twice and placebo twice, each in its own colour, order reversed for about half), then five sessions choosing which colour to take. People were told any capsule might hold a stimulant, a minor tranquilizer or a placebo, within the daily therapeutic range, and agreed to take no other drugs except usual coffee and cigarettes from 12 hours before to 6 hours after each capsule.

risk_of_bias.note: The claim is about which people choose benzodiazepines, a comparison between kinds of people. The contrast between people with and without histories of problem drug use is made across separate studies, by different laboratories, mostly at very different doses and with different procedures, so dose and procedure could explain it; the review reports that choice depended on dose but does not discuss this. The review's selection is unsystematic (card sc_griffiths_1997: high), 11 of its 13 drug-history studies are the first author's, and several of its labels rest on its own one-tailed re-tests. Within de Wit et al. (1986) anxious and non-anxious volunteers were compared at the same doses (RoB 2 some concerns on card sc_de_wit_1986: allocation to orders not described, staff blinding not stated, completers only, mood results tabulated only where significant).

inconsistency.note: Within each kind of person the direction is consistent: volunteers without problem drug use did not choose a benzodiazepine over placebo in any of the single-dose or capsule-by-capsule studies tabulated for them, and people with problem drug use chose it in every placebo-controlled study tabulated for them. The mixed results in anxious people and in insomnia line up with the procedure (a single morning dose against capsules as needed, or a forced choice against optional use), an explanation the review offers, untested, and the statement gives.

indirectness.note: Apart from de Wit et al. (1986), the evidence is second-hand, through one narrative review whose primary papers were not read. All the studies are laboratory or clinic studies from 1976 to 1997, mostly with single doses or single sessions of capsules prepared by the researchers, small samples and, among people with problem drug use, almost only men; what they show about choosing benzodiazepines outside a laboratory is not known.

imprecision.note: 2 to 16 people per study among people with problem drug use and about 10 to 14 per group in most other studies; the comparisons between kinds of people are small (de Wit et al.: 11 to 13 per group, no difference detected; anxious against other volunteers 65% against 45%, P = 0.06; moderate against light drinkers significant in one study of 27 people); no pooled estimate or interval.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a narrative review; the review does tabulate negative human studies, though not every negative animal study.

grade.reasoning: Rated as observational because the claim is about who chooses benzodiazepines, a comparison between kinds of people made mostly across separate studies (METHODS 6.3; brief for this round), although each study's own comparison of the drug with a placebo is within-person and mostly double-blind. Low start; risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 give very low (the scale stops there). The within-person finding of de Wit et al. (1986) alone, that 36 volunteers without problem drug use, anxious or not, mostly chose a placebo over single morning doses of diazepam, which calmed and sedated them without raising euphoria scores, rests on a counterbalanced, placebo-controlled comparison and a behavioural outcome and would be moderate on its own (high start; imprecision −1: 36 people, no intervals); the same laboratory found the same in other volunteers, as the review summarizes, which is replication by the same team. The contrast with people with problem drug use rests on the review's comparison of separate studies by another laboratory, mostly at much higher doses, and cannot separate history from dose; the statement says so and does not give it as the review's own caution, which it is not. Status replicated by the same team: volunteers without problem drug use were studied mainly by the Chicago group (de Wit, Johanson, Uhlenhuth) and people with problem drug use mainly by the review's first author's group, and no study read compared the two at the same doses. Choosing a drug over a placebo is not the same as feeling high: the review's definition of reinforcement covers any motive, and only de Wit et al. measured euphoria directly. The school-survey figure is second-hand and the national survey figure qualifies the claim without being part of the rating. The review's findings on how fast the drug acts and its comparisons of benzodiazepines by appeal are left out by design. Doses are given only as study conditions; nothing here is advice on amounts or use.

(1984b, J Pharmacol Exp Ther 229, 501–508), Johanson & Uhlenhuth (1980, Psychopharmacology 71, 269–273), Chutuape & de Wit (1995, Psychopharmacology 121, 91–103), Roache et al. (1996, Exp Clin Psychopharmacol 4, 308–314) and the survey report behind the high-school figure (Johnston, O'Malley & Bachman, 1993, NIH Publication No. 93-3597); no laboratory study after 1997 was read, and none compared people with and without problem drug use at the same doses. Left out by design: the review's findings on speed of onset (formulations and dosing patterns compared for liking and euphoria), its comparisons of benzodiazepines by appeal, and its animal studies. The review does not itself caution that the drug-history contrast is confounded with dose (the round brief's wording); the statement gives this as the editors' reading of its Tables 2 and 3 and of its own remark that choice depended on dose. Reference record de-wit_1986 lists one author and page 533; the PDF has five authors (de Wit, Uhlenhuth, Hedeker, McCracken, Johanson) and pages 533–541.

statement: Among US civilian adults living in households in 2015 and 2016, past-year misuse of benzodiazepines (any use other than as a doctor directed, by self-report) was reported by 2.2% (95% CI 2.0 to 2.3), against 10.4% (10.1 to 10.7) who reported using them only as prescribed; the people reporting misuse most often gave relaxing or relieving tension (47.1%) or help with sleep (26.6%) as their main reason, and getting high less often (11.6%), and most often got the pills from a friend or relative (68.8% in all, editors' sum). Certainty: low. Status: single study. The figures come from the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), a national probability survey answered by computer, partly in a private audio-assisted section meant to encourage honest answers, in 86,186 adults (Maust et al., 2019). In all, 12.6% (12.2 to 12.9) reported past-year benzodiazepine use, an estimated 30.6 million adults a year, so misuse made up 17.2% of use (5.3 million people against 25.3 million). Misuse counted taking a benzodiazepine without a prescription and taking one's own in greater amounts, more often or for longer than prescribed, and anyone reporting any misuse in the past year counted as misusing even if they also took it as prescribed. It was most common at ages 18 to 25 (5.2% of all adults that age; 51.0% of their benzodiazepine use) and least common at 65 or older (0.6%). Of the 2,533 people reporting misuse, 73.9% had taken a benzodiazepine without a prescription; the one misused was most often alprazolam (Xanax; 75.1%), then diazepam (20.5%), clonazepam (20.0%) and lorazepam (15.4%), some people naming more than one. Their main reasons, from a list: to relax or relieve tension 47.1%, to help with sleep 26.6%, to get high 11.6%, to help with feelings or emotions 10.1%, to experiment 6.0%, to increase or decrease the effects of another drug 1.6%, and 'hooked or have to have it' 0.6%. These shares add to 103.6% (editors' sum; 104.0% at ages 18 to 49 and 101.3% at 50 or older), more than rounding can explain, and 'another reason', also on the list, is not shown; the paper does not say whether people could give more than one main reason, so the shares cannot be read as exactly one reason per person. Getting high was the main reason for 13.9% at ages 18 to 49 and 3.0% at 50 or older, and sleep for 22.4% and 41.7%. Sources: free from a friend or relative 53.2%, bought from one 12.3% and stolen from one 3.3%, one doctor 19.5%, two or more doctors 0.9%, bought from a dealer or stranger 7.7%, and stolen from a health care setting 0.1% (together 97.0%, editors' sum; the rest not shown). Of the people reporting misuse, 4.6% (3.7 to 5.6) met DSM-IV criteria for past-year abuse and 6.8% (5.6 to 8.2) for past-year dependence, and they reported a mean of 5.4 days of misuse in the past month (whether people with no misuse that month are counted is not stated). Among people who used benzodiazepines, misuse rather than use as prescribed went with younger age, being male, and use, misuse or use disorders of alcohol, marijuana, prescription opioids and prescription stimulants, a cross-sectional association that shows nothing about cause. All of it is self-report without checks; adults in institutions and on active military duty are not covered; response rates are not given; and the 2015 redesign of the survey means the figures cannot be compared with earlier years. The authors suggest that part of what the survey counts as misuse may be people treating anxiety or insomnia that has gone untreated because of poor access to care; the analysis did not test this.
plain: Why do people misuse benzos like Xanax? In a big US survey in 2015 and 2016, about 13 in 100 adults said they had taken a benzodiazepine in the past year, and about 2 in 100 said they had misused one, meaning any use a doctor did not direct, such as taking pills without a prescription (the most common kind) or taking more of their own than prescribed. Three in four of the people who misused one had misused alprazolam (Xanax). Asked for their main reason, 47 in 100 said to relax or relieve tension, 27 in 100 to sleep, 12 in 100 to get high and 10 in 100 to cope with feelings; these shares add up to a little over 100, and the paper does not explain why. About 69 in 100 got the pills from a friend or relative, mostly for free. About 7 in 100 of the people who misused benzos met the criteria for dependence. These are people's own answers, not checked, and the survey did not include people in prisons, hospitals or the military.
population: US civilian adults aged 18 or older living in households, National Survey on Drug Use and Health 2015 and 2016 (86,186 respondents; 10,290 reporting past-year benzodiazepine use; 2,533 reporting misuse, 2,357 of them aged 18 to 49 and 176 aged 50 or older); people in institutions and on active military duty not covered
exposure: Self-reported past-year benzodiazepine use, only as prescribed or with misuse (any use other than as a doctor directed: without a prescription, or in greater amounts, more often or longer than prescribed), reported in the survey's tranquilizer and sedative sections
comparator: None for the shares among people reporting misuse (descriptive); use only as prescribed, for the share of use that was misuse and for the factors that went with misuse; ages 18 to 49 against 50 or older
outcome: Self-reported past-year use and misuse; among people reporting misuse, its type, main reason (from a list), source and the benzodiazepine misused; days of misuse in the past month; DSM-IV abuse and dependence
magnitude: Maust et al. (2019), NSDUH 2015–2016, survey-weighted: past-year any use 12.6% (95% CI 12.2–12.9), 30.6 million adults a year (29.7–31.5 million); only as prescribed 10.4% (10.1–10.7), 25.3 million (24.5–26.1); misuse 2.2% (2.0–2.3), 5.3 million (5.0–5.6); misuse 17.2% of use. Misuse by age, all adults: 18–25 5.2% (4.8–5.6), 26–34 3.3%, 35–49 1.7%, 50–64 1.4%, 65 or older 0.6% (0.4–0.8); as a share of use 51.0%, 28.6%, 13.8%, 9.7% and 4.4%. Among 2,533 reporting misuse (Table 3): without a prescription 73.9%, in greater amounts 16.0%, more often 10.1%, longer 4.9%, other ways 18.7%. Main reason: relax or relieve tension 47.1%, help with sleep 26.6%, get high 11.6%, feelings or emotions 10.1%, experiment 6.0%, effects of another drug 1.6%, hooked 0.6% (sum 103.6%, editors' calculation); ages 18–49 against 50 or older: get high 13.9% against 3.0% (OR 0.19, p = .003; interval printed as .07 to 56), sleep 22.4% against 41.7% (OR 2.48, 1.83–3.35), relax 48.6% against 41.7% (OR 0.76, 0.53–1.08). Source: free from a friend or relative 53.2%, bought from one 12.3%, stolen from one 3.3% (68.8%, editors' sum), one clinician 19.5%, two or more clinicians 0.9%, bought from a dealer or stranger 7.7%, stolen from a health care setting 0.1% (97.0% in all, editors' sum). Medication misused: alprazolam 75.1%, diazepam 20.5%, clonazepam 20.0%, lorazepam 15.4%. DSM-IV past-year abuse 4.6% (3.7–5.6), dependence 6.8% (5.6–8.2); mean days of misuse in the past month 5.4 (SE 0.3). Misuse against use as prescribed, adjusted OR: 65 or older against 18–25 0.23 (0.15–0.34); women 0.74 (0.61–0.90); alcohol abuse or dependence 2.31 (1.73–3.09); marijuana abuse or dependence 2.39 (1.62–3.52); prescription opioid misuse 4.11 (3.26–5.18), abuse or dependence 4.81 (3.45–6.72), use as prescribed 0.69 (0.57–0.84); prescription stimulant misuse 2.46 (1.85–3.27), abuse or dependence 3.40 (1.72–6.70), use as prescribed 0.90 (0.74–1.09).

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Benzodiazepine Use or Misuse, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2015 and 2016 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH): a 50-state multistage area probability sample of the US civilian non-institutionalized population, administered by RTI International for SAMHSA, answered in two computer-assisted parts, one private and audio-assisted to encourage honest reporting of illicit drug use; 86,186 adults. Benzodiazepine use counted when named in the tranquilizer (anxiety or muscle spasm) and sedative (insomnia) items (10,290 people; details in an online supplement). Since the 2015 redesign misuse means any use other than as a doctor directed: without a prescription, in greater amounts, more often or longer than prescribed, or in any other way; anyone reporting any past-year misuse counts as misusing, even if they also used the drug as prescribed. People reporting misuse were asked its manner, their reasons (to relax, to experiment, to get high, for sleep, for emotions, to counter the effect of another drug, because they were hooked, or another reason) and the source; abuse and dependence by DSM-IV criteria.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence checklist moderate (card sc_maust_2019): a national probability sample, one instrument across both years and design-based weights, with a private computer section for drug questions; but everything is self-report without checks, response rates are not given, and misuse is defined broadly, putting taking extra of one's own prescription, taking a relative's pill to sleep and taking one to get high in one category, which the statement says. Under-reporting and non-response would more likely lower the misuse figure than change the order of reasons or sources. Not downgraded.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US adults living in households in 2015–2016, and benzodiazepines in general (three in four people who misused one had misused alprazolam), not Xanax alone and not other countries.

imprecision.note: 2,533 people reporting misuse and 86,186 respondents; intervals are narrow for the overall figures. The figures for ages 50 or older rest on 176 people and are given only as a comparison.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to an analysis of a national survey.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (prevalence, and self-reported reasons and sources, in a national survey): starts low and is never upgraded; not downgraded (see the domain notes). The reasons are people's own answers to a list and are worded as such; their printed shares add to 103.6%, which the statement says, so they cannot be read as exactly one reason per person, but the order (relaxing, then sleep, then getting high) does not depend on the extra 3.6 points. The associations with other substances are cross-sectional and show nothing about cause. The authors' suggestion that some misuse reflects poor access to care is given as their untested suggestion. The abstract's advice to monitor patients also prescribed opioids or stimulants is left out, because the paper's own Table 2 does not support it (prescribed opioid use went with lower odds of misuse, prescribed stimulant use with no difference). Status single study: one analysis of one survey's first two years after its redesign.

verification.flag_note: Question 11 (forums: 'Why is Xanax so addictive?', 'Why do people like Klonopin so much?'). The abstract's advice to monitor patients also prescribed stimulants or opioids is left out (it conflicts with Table 2). The online supplement (how benzodiazepines were identified in the tranquilizer and sedative items) was not on file; the paper gives no response rates for 2015–2016 and does not explain why the main-reason shares add to 103.6%. The file read is the online-first version (Psychiatric Services in Advance, 17 December 2018), so anchors give PDF pages; the version of record is 70(2), 97–106. Not read: later NSDUH years, which would show whether the pattern holds.
